name: Victor Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. It's all confidential, so you can give me your public line and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the stockman at Lindenhof Farm, which the Hartmann family owns. We milk 180 cows, and we grow potatoes and wheat on about 200 hectares. I start milking at half four, then feeding, then in spring and autumn I'm on the tractor for the potatoes. The cows wear collars that tell us when they're on heat or off their feed, and an app on my phone flags them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the Hartmanns treat me fairly, and I like a clean parlour. What wears me out is the early starts in winter, and potato harvest, when it's sixteen-hour days for three weeks. Klara, my girlfriend, says she forgets what I look like in October.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I like things settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a lot of noise about technology, and then a good worker is still a good worker. I'd say it over a drink with the lads from the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in good shape. The Hartmanns pay fairly, I've got about four months saved, and Klara's working at the primary school. My job is steady and the farm is doing all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep at it. Keep saving for a house deposit, we're aiming for a little place in Rosendorf in 2028. And I'd ask Klara to marry me next summer, which I've been planning anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything at all change in your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The collar app might get a bit smarter. That's helpful. Otherwise, same cows, same potatoes, same early starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any worry in the background?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Potato prices, a bit. Mr Hartmann says one bad year and he'll cut the potatoes back, which would cut my overtime. But we'd manage.

say: I'd say a **good worker** is still a good worker after all the noise.
I'd say it at the **young farmers' club** over a drink.
think: I'm in **good shape**, with fair pay and four months saved.
The **Hartmanns' farm** is doing all right.
do: Keep **saving** for a house in Rosendorf in 2028.
Ask Klara to **marry** him next summer.
Keep the **same routine** of milking and potatoes.
S0.quote: There's a lot of noise about technology, and then a good worker is still a good worker.
fieldNote: He has a **secure** job with a fair employer and a working partner.
His only background worry is **potato overtime**.
He values **steadiness** and plans life events in order.

steps.text: Keep milking and running potato harvest at Lindenhof
Save for a house deposit in Rosendorf by 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I can see that one happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses should be free to use what helps them, and workers should keep up. I'd say farming's always changed, from horses to tractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is mostly cows and tractors, which comes later. Mr Hartmann would use AI for ordering feed and planning the potato rotation, which he hates anyway. I might get asked to use more apps, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new apps when the Hartmanns bring them in. I'd do a short course on the herd software if the farm paid for it. And I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but fine. Like hearing the weather forecast for next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever worry about a robot milker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hartmann looked at one two years ago. It's 150,000 per box and we'd need three. If he bought them, I'd want to be the one who runs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Hartmann, actually. Mrs Hartmann does all the farm office work, the accounts and orders, and that's exactly the kind of thing on your card.

say: I'd say businesses should be **free** to use what helps them.
I'd remind people farming moved from **horses to tractors**.
think: My work is mostly **cows and tractors**, which changes later.
Mr Hartmann would use AI for **feed orders** and rotations.
do: Learn **new apps** when the Hartmanns bring them in.
Take a **herd software** course if the farm pays.
feel: A little **uneasy** but fine, like next month's **forecast**.
S1.quote: Mrs Hartmann does all the farm office work, the accounts and orders, and that's exactly the kind of thing on your card.
fieldNote: He supports **business freedom** to automate, in line with his views.
He sees the risk with **Mrs Hartmann**, whose desk work matches the card.
His reaction to a robot milker is to **run it**, not fight it.

steps.text: Learn the herd management apps the Hartmanns bring in
Keep saving towards the Rosendorf house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to stand on their own feet and get ready, not wait for the government. I'd also say it's a shock, and I'd not pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think by 2031 Mr Hartmann buys robot milkers and maybe a robot for the potatoes. Mr Hartmann would keep one person to watch the robot milkers, and I'd want it to be me, but his son Lukas is coming home from agricultural college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the Hartmanns now if I can do the robot milking manufacturer's course, which runs about two weeks. I'd hold off on the house until I know the job's safe, keep the deposit as savings. I'd still propose to Klara, but we'd do a small wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I like things settled, and this isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the AI takes over the farm office and the planning, not my milking. So I'd have three years to make myself the robot man before the robots come. That's a fair chance, if I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Klara's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Klara's a teaching assistant, and I've heard they might use AI tutors. Klara says children still need someone to tie their shoes and stop fights, so she's not too worried.

say: I'd say people should stand on their **own feet** and prepare.
I'd admit it's a **shock** and not pretend otherwise.
think: By **2031** Mr Hartmann buys robot milkers and keeps one person.
I'd compete with his son **Lukas** for that one job.
do: Ask to take the **robot milking course** now, about two weeks.
Hold off the **house** and keep the deposit as savings.
Still propose, but plan a **small wedding**.
S2.quote: Mr Hartmann would keep one person to watch the robot milkers, and I'd want it to be me, but his son Lukas is coming home from agricultural college.
fieldNote: His strategy is to become the **robot man** in the three-year gap.
The owner's son **Lukas** is a quiet threat to his place.

steps.text: Ask the Hartmanns to pay for a two-week robot milking course
Postpone the Rosendorf house and keep the deposit in savings
Propose to Klara and plan a small wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time enough for anyone willing to work. I'd tell younger lads to get skills, not complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for AI and robots around 2034 means I'd be 35. That's plenty of time to make myself useful with robots. The Hartmanns would buy them, and I'd run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robot milking course in 2028. I'd buy the house in Rosendorf on schedule. I'd start using the herd app properly now, all of its features.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit uneasy at the edges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Lukas earlier. Does he worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less so. With five years, Lukas and I could split the farm work, him in the office and me in the parlour. There's room for two if the farm grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Klara change family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We'd marry in 2027 and think about children after the house. Five years is enough to keep things in order.

say: I'd say five years is **time enough** for anyone willing to work.
I'd tell younger lads to **get skills**, not complain.
think: Robots around **2034** leave me time to become useful with them.
The Hartmanns would buy robots and **I'd run them**.
do: Use **every feature** of the herd app now.
feel: Mostly **fine**, a bit **uneasy** at the edges.
S3.quote: With five years, Lukas and I could split the farm work, him in the office and me in the parlour.
fieldNote: Five years removes his **rivalry worry** with the owner's son.
His **family plans** for marriage in 2027 and a house stay on schedule.
He frames adaptation as **personal effort**, not policy.

steps.text: Take the robot milking manufacturer's course in 2028
Buy the Rosendorf house on schedule
Use every feature of the cow collar app from now on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone who works on a farm. Anyone who gets caught out after a decade had their warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when AGI comes and 40 when robots arrive. By then I'd hope to be married, with children and a house, and running the Hartmanns' robots. I think I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married, buy the house, start a family. I'd pick up the tools as other farms prove them. Around 2033, I'd do whatever training the robot companies offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children farming is still a good life, but learn the machines as well as the animals. My grandfather did horses and tractors, and I'd do cows and robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would shake that calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the Hartmanns sold up. Then I'd be looking for work like everyone else. But they've farmed Lindenhof for four generations, so I doubt it.

say: I'd call ten years of warning a real **gift** for farm workers.
I'd say anyone **caught out** after a decade of warning had their chance.
think: By 40 I'd hope to be **running the robots** at Lindenhof.
I'd expect to be **married**, with children and a house.
do: Marry Klara, **buy the house** and start a family.
Pick up **tools** as other farms prove them.
S4.quote: My grandfather did horses and tractors, and I'd do cows and robots.
fieldNote: Ten years lets his **life plan** unfold without disruption.
His only shake point is the **Hartmanns selling**.
He uses **family history** to make change feel normal.

steps.text: Marry Klara, buy the house and start a family
Adopt new farm tools once neighbouring farms prove them

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have only three years to make myself useful with robots. What would help is apprenticeships on farms for running robots, paid for by the companies that sell them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about bosses. A good employer matters more than any machine. If the Hartmanns treat me fairly, I'll learn whatever they need.

headlineQuote: A good employer matters more than any machine.
portrait: Victor is a 27-year-old **stockman** at a family-run dairy and potato farm.
He uses AI **now and then**, through the cow collar app.
He believes in **self-reliance** and a fair employer.
He is **calm** in AI Plateau and **anxious** at AGI by 2028.
His plan is to become the farm's **robot man** while life plans continue.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, giving only three years to become useful with robots.
whatWouldHelp: **Farm apprenticeships** in running robots, paid for by the robot companies.
